Transcript body:
[00:00] Morgan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, quick roll call — I'm Morgan, AE at Redwood, and Diego (waves) is our SE, he'll do the deep sizing stuff.
[00:12] Anika Shah: Hi Morgan, Anika here. Thanks. We've got Tom and Priya on as well. We're eager to figure out how to make the POC feel like production so we can validate cost and latency.
[00:22] Tom Reynolds: Yup, Tom, infra. We run in GCP today, mostly T4/NV setups for research, but production is GKE + some managed GPUs, nothing consistent.
[00:28] Diego Ramos: Cool — so quick question, can you share your typical concurrency and token profiles? Rough numbers are fine.
[00:36] Priya Menon: Sure — average conversational session is about 6 turns, median tokens per request ~320, but we have a long-tail up to 2,000 tokens for summarization use cases. Peak concurrent requests today measure around 150-200 RPS on our staging.
[00:51] Morgan Lee: Okay, that's super helpful. For a POC we usually size for peak-ish plus a safety margin. Diego, are you thinking baseline reserved pool then burst?
[00:58] Diego Ramos: Yeah. For the numbers Anika gave — median 320 tokens and 200 RPS peak — we recommend starting the POC with a reserved pool sized for sustained baseline throughput. Rough calc: assuming an H100-class performance-ish profile - forgive my speak, I'm saying H-one-hundred - but if we assume ~70 tokens/sec per GPU for your model shape, to cover 20k tokens/sec sustained we'd need about 285 GPUs — sorry, that math is off. Let me rephrase, um, sorry.
[01:28] Diego Ramos: Real numbers: if your peak incoming token rate is 6,000 tokens/sec (200 RPS * 30 tokens/sec average per request) you'd need roughly 6-8 A100/H100 GPUs depending on model variant and quantization. For POC let's prototype with 4 reserved GPUs (A100 or H100 fractional), pre-warmed with KV cache for the common prefixes, and allow burst up to 8 GPUs from Redwood shared capacity.
[01:55] Tom Reynolds: That 4-reserved baseline — does that assume batching? We're fairly latency-sensitive, 95th latency SLO is 250ms for interactive flows.
[02:03] Diego Ramos: Good call. If latency is tight, we keep batching small. The baseline 4 reserved assumes small-batch mode and active KV caching so most requests hit lower latency. For strict 95th <= 250 ms we'll need to tune concurrency and pre-warm on the model warm path. If you need sub-200ms token latency we might need more reserved GPUs or lower parameter models.
[02:26] Anika Shah: For success criteria, we want <250ms 95th for 80% of production queries, cost per 1k tokens under $0.05, and no more than 2 outages for the POC window. Timeline-wise, we're hoping to validate in 4-6 weeks.
[02:40] Morgan Lee: Sounds reasonable. We'll codify that as SLOs: 95th P95 < 250ms for interactive endpoints, cost target as you said.
[02:48] Priya Menon: One extra constraint — data residency. Some of our customers require EU-only storage, so if we do private deployment we need VPC + KMS keys in eu-west1.
[02:58] Morgan Lee: Noted. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and a VPC control plane; we'll include a note in the security pack.
[03:05] Tom Reynolds: What about burst policy — what's the cooldown and how quickly can you scale up? We can't have sudden latency cliffs.
[03:12] Diego Ramos: Two parts: autoscaling and fallback. Autoscaling into Redwood's shared pool can burst up within ~60-120 seconds depending on inventory and GPU type. We suggest a mixed strategy for POC: reserved baseline (always there), a fast burst policy to draw from the shared pool for short spikes (pre-warm script triggers model loading), and a graceful fallback to a smaller model variant or emulated region fallback if capacity is exhausted. For example, primary route -> reserved H100s; fallback route -> redwood-compact-v2 in a different region which has lower latency but is cheaper and faster to spin up.
[03:48] Anika Shah: Hm, region fallback sounds risky for us due to GDPR. Can we instead fallback to a quantized variant in the same region?
[03:54] Diego Ramos: Absolutely — same-region quantized variants are the preferred pattern for data-sensitive teams. So fallback to a 4-bit quantized variant on the same infra; less quality but keeps data in-region.
[04:06] Morgan Lee: Also we can configure rollout policies: if latency or error rate crosses thresholds, traffic shifts incrementally to fallback; we avoid sudden cutovers.
[04:14] Tom Reynolds: What's the billing model during bursts? Do we bill for actual GPU time or a flat premium?
[04:20] Morgan Lee: For POC we propose a blended model: reserved capacity at a fixed monthly POC rate pro-rated, plus usage-based billing for burst minutes. We'll send a concrete quote. POC pricing typically includes a capped burst budget to make costs predictable.
[04:33] Priya Menon: On benchmarks — we want a reproducible 1-hour stress run that mirrors our 95th percentile. Diego, can you outline the bench steps?
[04:41] Diego Ramos: Yes. We'll ask you to upload traces (RPS by second, tokens per request, sequence lengths). Our bench runbook: 1) import traces into Redwood bench driver, 2) run a warmup for 10 minutes with KV cache priming, 3) run a 45 minute steady-state at 95th profile, 4) simulate spikes with 30s bursts to 2x RPS. We'll capture per-token latency, GPU occupancy, and tail latencies. We'll share the spreadsheet results.
[05:08] Anika Shah: Great. For the POC success criteria — can you give acceptance gates? Like 'if 95th latency <= 250ms and cost <= target' we move to pilot?
[05:16] Morgan Lee: We'll create an acceptance checklist: (1) performance gate: 95th <= 250ms for interactive endpoints during bench, (2) cost gate: estimated monthly cost within 10% of target when scaled, (3) stability gate: no more than 2 critical errors during bench, (4) security gate: VPC + KMS proof-of-concept deployed or security docs reviewed. If all pass, we move to a 3-month pilot with reserved capacity commit.
[05:40] Tom Reynolds: A couple of nitty-gritty questions — how do you handle KV cache consistency across scaled replicas? We use conversation affinity for session state.
[05:48] Diego Ramos: Redwood supports per-session affinity and shared KV cache options. For POC we'd likely use sticky sessions to pin a user's KV to a warm replica; we can also configure async replication for cold-start mitigation. There's a small consistency window but it's usually acceptable for conversational contexts. We'll show config examples in the bench runbook.
[06:08] Priya Menon: Any limit on sequence length with quantized models? Our summarization goes to 2k tokens frequently.
[06:15] Diego Ramos: Quantized variants can handle 2k but you may see higher latency and lower throughput. For summarization-heavy routes we recommend routing to a larger model or batching those jobs as async pipelines. The POC can test both sync interactive and async summarization flows.
[06:30] Anika Shah: Security — SOC2, audit logs, SSO. We'll need SAML + RBAC for the console.
[06:36] Morgan Lee: We support SAML SSO and role-based access. Audit logs are available and can be streamed to your SIEM. We'll attach SOC2 report and our security pack to the follow-up email.
[06:46] Tom Reynolds: Anything else we should be aware of, like kernel selection or CUDA quirks?
[06:50] Diego Ramos: Minor note: certain operator kernels behave differently on older drivers; for the POC we'll recommend driver level X.Y and provide a pre-warm script that pins kernels to avoid jitter. We'll include the script in the runbook.
[07:05] Morgan Lee: Ok, timeline recap — you send traces by the 15th, Redwood sends pricing by the 11th, Diego will run bench around the 18th. POC duration target 4-6 weeks.
[07:16] Priya Menon: That aligns with our internal timeline.
[07:20] Anika Shah: Quick question — if during the POC we see model quality regression when using quantized fallback, do you support automated rollbacks?
[07:28] Diego Ramos: Yes — Redwood Optimize monitors quality via prompt sets and you can configure automatic rollback to the last known-good model if quality drops beyond a threshold. We'll include an example of an eval threshold in the runbook.
[07:41] Tom Reynolds: Last one: can we limit burst to certain hours only? We have maintenance windows outside business hours.
[07:47] Morgan Lee: Absolutely — burst windows and capacity caps are configurable per route. We'll include a sample policy: weekdays 8-20 UTC burst enabled, nights disabled.
[07:56] Priya Menon: Thanks — that's helpful.
[07:59] Morgan Lee: Cool. Any blockers on next steps?
[08:02] Anika Shah: None from my side. We'll gather and share traces.
[08:06] Tom Reynolds: I'll get the trace export done.
[08:09] Morgan Lee: Great — we'll follow up with the pricing and the runbook and schedule the bench slot. Thanks all.
